newsitem.title: UK: Focus-British Airways talks strike is illegal.
newsitem.headline: Focus-British Airways talks strike is illegal.

text.p: British Airways said on Wednesday the cabin crew strike that has crippled its services out of London was illegal and it had consulted lawyers on possible legal action.
The airline says discrepancies in the strike ballot make the action by the Transport and General Workers Union (T&G) illegal. More than half of its flights from the capital have been grounded.
"We are now in active discussions with our legal advisers," Mervyn Walker, BA director of human resources, told a news conference.
"We have the right to damages in respect of losses we incur, and to other legal remedies."
BA shares ended 19-1/2 pence higher at 692-1/2 on Wednesday. Analysts and traders said the shares shot up on hopes that strike would be settled quickly.
British Airways also insisted it would not negotiate the terms of a deal to cut costs by 42 million pounds ($71 milion) that triggered the dispute.
The union has said it is prepared to help the airline find the money, but it is not prepared to have new terms and conditions imposed on its members.
It also disputed BA's claim that the 72-hour strike that is due to continue until Saturday morning was illegal.
"We have absolute confidence in the legality of our conduct," said union spokesman Andrew Murray told Reuters. "There is no change in the union position."
Walker, who insists the only way to achieve the cuts is through the deal presented to the union, said another possible option for the airline was a legal injunction.
The cabin crew strike began at 0500 GMT on Wednesday, forcing the airline to cancel between 20 and 30 percent of the 1,000 flights it operates worldwide each day.
Pickets carrying banners gathered in the early morning sun near BA's headquarters at Heathrow, while usually frenetic Terminal One was eerily quiet.
Pickets were also stationed outside other British airports and some were even flown to New York to try to win support from workers there.
British Airways said late on Wednesday that 874 cabin staff had reported to work as normal and it expected the number to increase to about 1000 by the end of the day.
More than 1500 had called in sick, rather than strike, because of fears of crossing a picket line. Another 160 have been officially on strike.
The airline needs between 1,800-2,000 staff to run a full programme on a normal day.
"It is clear to us now that the strike is not well supported," said Kevin Murray, BA director of communications. "A large number of crew are coming into work."

Asked whether the crew had reported sick rather than go on strike because of BA's threats that strikers would lose perks and face a lockout, Walker said: "Crew have not been threatened. We have not intimidated and never would intimidate any of our employees."
The airline said it hoped to operate 20 percent more flights on Thursday, but haven't yet specified what services they will be able to run.
